stt: Ask HN: Which book have you re-read recently?
x:
I'm in love with Rethinking Innateness. I'm posting half in the hope someone suggests an up to date version, but it's brilliant and fascinating itself. It was prescribed when I was studying my CS MSc and I've read it three times now.

I got initially into computers because I would press something on the keyboard and knew there was a sequence of commands that directed the graphics card to output something – I needed to understand that. Now, as I assume applies to so many people here, my curiosity has expanded to human development, this books is _the bridge_ between CS and psychology.

https://www.amazon.com/Rethinking-Innateness-Connectionist-P...
See my post in another thread re Elman et al. Rethinking Innateness (https://mitpress.mit.edu/books/rethinking-innateness).

What you're looking for is Elman et al's theory in Rethinking Innateness (https://mitpress.mit.edu/books/rethinking-innateness) It's more like Darwin than Newton, and is (to the point of another post off this thread) an early deep-learning-like theory of how the brain (or at least the cortex) becomes organized.

stt: I'm an Old Fart and AI Makes Me Sad
x:
An update on Minsky's proof.  It was correctly formulated but based on a too limited model.  Adding location into the model allows learning XOR.

I demonstrated this with Hebbian learning on a Hopfield network finding learning of up to 6 dimensional XORs.  This was a replication of work by Elman and reported in Rethinking Innateness[0].

A more provocative claim: layers and back propagation, despite providing us with fantastic advancements, are unnecessary.

[0] https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262050524/rethinking-innateness...
